one_liner: Java JSON databinding library with compile-time generated converters; about 2x nlohmann/json and json-c in kostya's JSON test, far behind fast C/C++ parsers.
what_it_does: DSL-JSON serialises and deserialises JVM objects (Java, Kotlin, Scala, Android) to and from UTF-8 byte[] or streams. An annotation processor generates converters at compile time for classes marked @CompiledJson and for the classes they reference, with a reflection-based runtime mode as fallback. It is a schema-bound databinding API (JSON straight into your POJOs), not a DOM like nlohmann::json or json-c, and it deliberately has no String API.
how_it_is_fast: Generated converters read the byte[] directly with no intermediate char or String form, match property names by a hash of their bytes rather than by string comparison, skip unknown properties without materialising them, and allocate almost nothing beyond the target objects (README FAQ: almost zero allocations, byte-level work, minimised branching, compile-time databinding instead of reflection). In the benchmarked 2.0.2 release, numbers of up to 15 + precision-level characters are parsed by a hand-written digit loop with an approximate correction step, and longer ones fall back to Double.parseDouble on a new String; master (2026-10-06, unreleased) replaces this with an exact Ryu-style parser.
when_to_use: Java or Kotlin services that bind known JSON shapes into POJOs and want one of the fastest JVM codecs without leaving Java (0.571 s in kostya's JSON test against 1.18-1.27 s for nlohmann/json and json-c).
Android or Java 8 targets: v2 targets Java 8 and the README documents Android Gradle setup.
Large arrays of small objects where only a few fields matter: unknown fields are skipped, not built, and the streaming iterateOver API reads big lists with little memory.
Codecs that must avoid reflection at runtime, since converters are generated and discovered through META-INF/services.
when_not_to_use: You can call C or C++: simdjson On-Demand (0.060 s), DAW JSON Link (0.070-0.089 s), yyjson (0.131 s), RapidJSON (0.154 s), Boost.JSON (0.374 s) and yajl (0.362 s) all beat it on the same test, and so does jsoniter-scala on the JVM (0.147 s).
Arbitrary or schema-less JSON: the fast path needs compile-time types; the reflection mode is described by the authors as only comparable to Jackson.

Memory-tight processes: the JVM row used 277.81 MiB base plus 163.69 MiB peak, against 113 MiB base for the C/C++ rows; only the DOM-building C++ libraries (nlohmann +360-448 MiB, json-c +1,216 MiB) used more on top.
You need a maintained release: the last release on Maven Central is 2.0.2 (2023-08-29); fixes since then, including a double-parsing crash and the Ryu parser, are on master only.
Strict input validation or security-sensitive parsing without review: open issues report spec-profile misses for 2.0.2 (#300) and an XXE path in XmlConverter (#296).

integration.form: Maven jar (com.dslplatform:dsl-json) with a bundled annotation processor
integration.dependencies: none at runtime for the core jar (README: about 450KB); the JSON-B API is a provided dependency for JsonB support; Kotlin uses the same artifact through kapt, Scala needs dsl-json-scala
integration.min_toolchain: Java 8 (v2 targets Java 8); the kostya build compiles with javac -proc:full so the processor on the classpath runs
integration.platforms: any JVM, Android; Kotlin via kapt; Scala via dsl-json-scala
integration.thread_safety: README: create one DslJson and always reuse it; its serialize and deserialize methods reuse readers and writers through thread-local variables, while a JsonReader or JsonWriter you create via newReader/newWriter is a single-owner object

gotchas: The comparison is not like-for-like: the Java test binds only coordinates[].x/y/z into generated classes and skips name, opts and info, while the nlohmann driver builds a full std::map DOM (and destroys it inside the timed call) and json-c builds a tree it never frees; RapidJSON SAX Precise (0.433-0.500 s), the closest C++ shape, is still faster than DSL-JSON's 0.571 s.

Correction to the record's reading of DoublePrecision.LOW: in 2.0.2 it only raises the fast-path length limit to 19 characters (15 + level 4). The x and y values in the generated file are exponent-form doubles of about 21-22 characters, so they still go through Double.parseDouble on a new String, and only z (about 18-19 characters) takes the approximate path; the suite's README flags reduced-precision C/C++ variants but not this setting, and the output is printed to %g without a cross-language check.

Released 2.0.2 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in NumberConverter.approximateDouble on some doubles such as 2E15 or 2670986322885633.0 (issue #283); the maintainer says it works on master (2026-10-10), which has no release.

The benchmark constructs a new DslJson with includeServiceLoader inside every timed calc call and runs a single cold parse with no JIT warm-up, contrary to the README's advice to reuse the instance; both choices count against Java, so the 2x over nlohmann is not inflated by them. Properties are matched by hash by default (hashMatch), so a colliding unknown name can land in the wrong field unless hashMatch is turned off.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against JSON3.jl, the other catalogued kostya JSON entry (0.700 s, 631.76 + 332.81 MiB), DSL-JSON is faster and lighter on the same test; pick it when the code base is Java or Kotlin, and pick jsoniter-scala (0.147 s, catalogued under JSON) instead for Scala, or a C++ binder such as simdjson On-Demand or DAW JSON Link when native code is an option.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks' JSON test (parse a 524,288-object pretty-printed file and average x, y, z; median of runs on an Intel Xeon E-2324G, update 2026-07-19) timed DSL-JSON 2.0.2 on HotSpot with default flags (JDK 24.0.2 per the README, 26.0.1 per the current Dockerfile) at 0.571 s against nlohmann/json at 1.182 s (clang++ 22.1.8) and 1.266 s (g++ 16.1.0), json-c at 1.185-1.187 s and Boost.PropertyTree at 2.589-2.907 s, all built -O3 -march=native -flto=auto; the gain is schema binding versus DOM building, not Java codegen.
status_note: BSD-3-Clause, 1.1k stars and 422 commits; master is active again in 2026 (Ryu number parsing, XML security fixes, skipNullValues) after almost no commits between August 2023 and June 2026, but the last published release is still 2.0.2 from 2023-08-29 with 41 open issues, so pin a version and test your number edge cases.
